title: CFA Ethics 48: Case - launching a new fund, and everything that can go wrong in the offering document
subtitle: Simulated performance, designations, benchmarks and promises - four standards in one set of materials
whyItMatters: An offering document is where more standards intersect in a single product than anywhere else, and where commercial pressure is highest - which makes it the right combined case to close the ethics section with.
openingQuestion: A new fund's offering document states: "the strategy returned 18% a year over 2019-2024" - where 2019-2022 is backtested. Where is the problem?
openingOptions: No problem, provided the simulation was computed with a sound method
Misrepresentation: merging simulation and live operation into one line
It is only a problem if the simulated period produced the higher result
The only problem is not stating whether fees have been deducted
explanation: A single figure spanning both periods sends the message that the strategy has been running continuously for six years, when in the first four not a single dong was actually invested and the parameters were chosen after the results were known. Standard III(D) requires fair, accurate and complete presentation - and all three are breached here: not fair, because simulation and live results are not the same kind of evidence; not complete, because the reader cannot tell which is which; and not accurate in what it implies, however correct each individual figure may be.

summary.keyIdea: Merging simulated results with live results breaches all three of III(D)'s requirements at once - complete, fair, and not misleading.
summary.commonMistake: Adding a small note that part of it is simulated and treating that as transparency. If the two kinds sit on one line on the chart, a footnote does not repair the impression.

application.title: How to present it properly
application.message: Separate the two periods entirely, state the date live operation began, and set out every assumption behind the simulated portion.

sections.text: Launching a new fund is when the offering document gets written under the pressure of raising capital. It is also when Standard III(D) on performance presentation is most often breached - usually not by a wrong number.

The strategy was backtested for four years and has run live for two, and the document presents one continuous six-year performance line. Each individual figure may be correct, but the message is wrong: the reader understands that the strategy has been running for six years, when in the first four not a single dong was actually invested and the parameters were chosen after the results were known.

sections.label: Three requirements breached at once
sections.text: Not fair - simulation and live results are not the same kind of evidence. Not complete - the reader cannot tell which is which. Not accurate in what it implies, however verifiable each individual figure may be.
The other three faults in the same set of materials

items: The wrong kind of benchmark: comparing a small-cap equity fund with a large-cap index is misrepresentation without a single wrong number.
Use of the CFA designation: Standard VII(B) applies in full to marketing materials, with no exception for sales purposes.
Claims about the team's capability: every assertion under Standard I(C) must be verifiable, including sentences that read like ordinary advertising.

sections.text: One point often missed: if the document claims GIPS compliance, that claim carries obligations at firm level rather than for the fund being offered - and where those are not met, the claim itself is the violation.

lines: Not one figure in this set of materials is wrong.
But the picture they paint does not exist.

diagram.label: III(D): merging simulation with live results is misrepresentation
VII(B): the team's designations must describe their actual status
V(B): the benchmark must be the same asset class
I(C): every claim about capability must be verifiable

realWorldExample.company: The benchmark is the easiest place to mislead and the hardest to catch
realWorldExample.description: Choosing an index that is easy to beat as the benchmark gets no number wrong, but it turns an average result into outperformance on paper. Standard V(B) requires the process and the basis to be stated, and the requirement that a benchmark be the same asset class, the same segment and the same risk level sits inside that. Comparing a mid-cap equity fund with a deposit rate is the extreme example; comparing it with a large-cap index is far subtler and far more common.

quiz.question: Merging simulated performance with live performance breaches which standard?
options: III(D) - performance presentation
V(A) - diligence and reasonable basis
VI(A) - disclosure of conflicts
IV(B) - additional compensation
quiz.explanation: All three of III(D)'s requirements - fair, accurate, complete - are breached at once by this presentation.

quiz.question: Why is choosing an easy-to-beat benchmark a problem?
options: Because the rules mandate one index per fund type
Because it turns an average result into outperformance on paper
Because the benchmark directly determines the performance fee
Because investors have no way of checking that index
quiz.explanation: This is the subtlest form of misrepresentation: every number is correct and still leads the reader to a wrong conclusion.

quiz.question: A fund team member has passed all three levels but lacks the required experience. How should that be stated?
options: Write "CFA (pending)" to show the final stage
Write "CFA", since all the exams have been completed
Describe the actual status, without using the CFA designation
Say nothing at all about progress through the CFA programme
quiz.explanation: Standard VII(B) applies in full to marketing materials - and this is where commercial pressure most often pushes people too far.

quiz.question: The claim "the team has 50 years of combined experience" falls under which standard?
options: VI(B) - priority of transactions
III(A) - loyalty, prudence and care
IV(C) - the responsibilities that fall on a supervisor
I(C) - claims of capability must be verifiable
quiz.explanation: Adding several people's experience together is not wrong in itself, but it has to be accurate and must not create an impression of depth that does not exist.

quiz.question: If a fund claims GIPS compliance, what necessarily comes with it?
options: The whole firm must comply, not this fund alone
Only this fund needs to be verified by an independent party
Only the fund's performance methodology needs disclosing
Only at least five years of live operating history is needed
quiz.explanation: Firm-level compliance is the foundational rule of GIPS, and it exists precisely to prevent the label being attached to the best-looking product.

keyTakeaways: Merging simulation with live operation breaches all three requirements of III(D)
The wrong kind of benchmark is misrepresentation without a single wrong number
VII(B) applies in full to marketing materials
Every claim about the team's capability must be verifiable under I(C)
A GIPS claim carries obligations at firm level

practicePrompt.question: The sales team wants "target return of 15% a year" on the cover of the document. How do you respond?
options: Agree, since it is a target rather than a commitment
State clearly that it is a target with its assumptions, not a promise
Refuse, since all forward-looking figures are prohibited
Agree, provided a disclaimer is added to the footer of every page
practicePrompt.explanation: Standard V(B) does not prohibit stating a target - it requires fact to be separated clearly from opinion and the underlying assumptions to be stated. A footer disclaimer is the most common approach and it does not meet the standard, because placement and prominence are part of whether a disclosure is meaningful at all.
